sources.title: Emily Dickinson (English Wikipedia) -- orientation only; not used as support for any scored row.

Emily Dickinson (Q4441) -- verified live via wbgetentities (2026-10-02): en label 'Emily Dickinson', description 'American poet (1830-1886)', ko label '에밀리 디킨슨', kowiki '에밀리 디킨슨', born 1830-12-10, died 1886-05-15, citizenship Q30 (United States), P18 'Emily Dickinson daguerreotype (Restored, cropped, blown up, sepia).jpg' (not used). Orientation only.

Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 'Emily Dickinson's Letters', The Atlantic Monthly vol. 68 (October 1891), read in its reprint as ch. XIX 'Emily Dickinson' (pp. 247-283) of Higginson, Carlyle's Laugh and Other Surprises (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1909), archive.org OCR (carlyleslaughoth00higg), read in full -- FIRSTHAND CORRESPONDENT perspective (non-self narrative; he was her literary correspondent 1862-1886, met her in Amherst on 16 Aug. 1870 and once more, and co-edited her posthumous Poems 1890-91, so an interested party and an admirer). Contains his own account plus her letters to him as he printed them (her letters are counted as SELF material, see the record of Dickinson's own letters). Read: the 15/16 April 1862 first letter with four poems and the name on a separate pencilled card; his 'surgery' (criticism) and her replies of 25 April, 7 June and July 1862 (declining his advice to delay publishing; 'will you be my preceptor'); his attempt to steer her toward rules and her reply that she corrected spelling but not 'greater irregularities'; his observation that she would not change word order to gain a rhyme; the 1862-63 wartime letters; his statement that he 'soon abandoned all attempt to guide' her; two letters asking him to support her refusals to contribute (a charity request; Helen Hunt Jackson's 1876 'No Name Series' request); her invitations and 'I do not cross my father's ground to any house or town'; his account, from notes taken at the time, of the 16 Aug. 1870 interview; her letters after her father's death (1874) and Bowles's death (1878). Her statements about illness, eyes and bereavement were read and not used for any row.

Mabel Loomis Todd, editorial prefaces -- (a) Preface (signed Amherst, Aug. 1891) to Poems by Emily Dickinson, Second Series, ed. T. W. Higginson and M. L. Todd (Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1891), archive.org OCR (poemsbyemilyd00dickrich), pp. 3-8, read in full; (b) 'Introductory' (signed Amherst, Oct. 1894) to Letters of Emily Dickinson, ed. Todd, 2 vols. (Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1894), archive.org OCR (lettersofemilydi00dick), pp. v-xii, read in full -- EDITOR perspective (non-self; Todd knew the family and worked from the manuscripts after Dickinson's death but, by her own account elsewhere, never met her face to face; she had a personal and commercial stake in the editions, so an interested party). Used for her description of the manuscripts found after Dickinson's death: most poems 'carefully copied on sheets of note-paper, and tied in little fascicules, each of six or eight sheets'; many showing 'thoughtful revision' with 'foot-notes, affording large choice of words and phrases'; different versions sent to different friends; the editors' judgement that she 'intentionally avoided the smoother and more usual rhymes'; Helen Hunt Jackson's letter of 5 Sept. 1884 urging her to publish ('you will not give them light'); and that she kept no journal, rarely addressed her own envelopes in later years and gave up journeys. Todd's assertions about Dickinson's temperament, religion and reasons for seclusion are editorial characterisation and were NOT used.

Emily Dickinson Museum (Amherst, Mass.), 'The Poet at Work' section, five pages read in full 2026-10-02: 'The Poet at Work' (writing table in her bedroom; drafts on envelopes and scrap paper; forty hand-made booklets holding more than 800 poems, found after her death), 'The Manuscripts' (about 2,500 poem manuscripts and 1,000 letter manuscripts; 1858-1864 copying of 800+ poems into forty fascicles she made herself by stacking folded sheets, stabbing two holes and tying with string; fifteen unbound 'sets'; retained copies; about 500 poems shared with more than forty correspondents; 'A Route of Evanescence' sent to at least six recipients; about 100 fragments/worksheets), 'Publications in Dickinson's Lifetime' (one letter and ten poems, 1850-1878, all anonymous, scholars believe none authorised), 'The Publication Question' (Helen Hunt Jackson's 1878 Masque of Poets placement and her rebuke for refusing to publish; Thomas Niles's approach, which she avoided answering; the c.1880 charity request), and 'The Posthumous Discovery of Dickinson's Poems' (Lavinia's discovery; Todd-Higginson 1890 editorial alterations to punctuation, titles and words for rhyme; later editions by Bianchi, Johnson 1955, Franklin 1981/1998) -- MUSEUM/SCHOLARLY perspective, modern and independent of the 1890s editors (it cites Franklin, Johnson, Bianchi and Scharnhorst). The page's passing reference to the Todd-Austin Dickinson relationship is not used.

Emily Dickinson Museum (Amherst, Mass.), biography section pages read in full 2026-10-02: '1855-1865: The Writing Years' (1858-1865 composing, revising and saving hundreds of poems; c. 800 recorded in hand-made fascicles shared with no one; c. 250 poems to Susan Dickinson and c. 100 to Higginson; her own bedroom as writing space; 1864-65 Boston eye treatment, after which she rarely left the Homestead grounds), '1865-1886: The Later Years' (stopped formal assembly of booklets; Higginson's 1875 reading; Helen Hunt Jackson's 'no name' request, L573a; the 1878 Masque of Poets), 'Emily Dickinson and Gardening' (gardening throughout her life; conservatory; school-years herbarium of more than 400 specimens each labelled with its Latin name, now Houghton Library), 'Emily Dickinson's Schooling: Mount Holyoke Female Seminary' (1847-48; placed by examination, promoted by midterm; listed among those 'without hope' at entry and among 29 who remained so at year end; her letter to Abiah Root, L20), 'Emily Dickinson and the Church' (did not make the public profession of faith during the revivals when family and friends did; had stopped attending services by 1868), and 'Emily Dickinson and Reading' (wide reading; daily Springfield Republican and every issue of the Atlantic; Bible and Shakespeare) -- MUSEUM/SCHOLARLY perspective, modern, citing Habegger, Sewall, Leyda, Capps, Longsworth, Franklin. The pages' material on health, the 'Master Letters', the 'terror' of 1861-62 and Judge Lord was read and deliberately NOT used.

T. W. Higginson's CONTEMPORANEOUS private letters to his wife Mary Channing Higginson, Amherst 'Tuesday 10 P.M.' (16 Aug. 1870, Johnson no. 342a) and White River Junction 'Wednesday noon' (17 Aug. 1870, no. 342b, with the enclosed sheet of notes on E.D.), his diary entry of 16 Aug. 1870 and the postscript to his sisters of 21 Aug. 1870, all as printed from the Boston Public Library and Houghton manuscripts in Johnson and Ward (eds.), The Letters of Emily Dickinson, vol. II (see the record of the Johnson and Ward edition of the letters), pp. 472-476, read in full -- FIRSTHAND VISITOR perspective (non-self; same witness as the record of Higginson's 1891 Atlantic Monthly essay, so NOT counted as an independent perspective, but written the same night rather than 21 years later, and private). Used: his description of the meeting; that she talked 'continuously -- & deferentially'; that she bakes all the bread because her father likes only hers; that she said she never left the place and never felt want of employment; his own reaction ('I never was with any one who drained my nerve power so much ... I am glad not to live near her') and that 'She often thought me tired & seemed very thoughtful of others'. Her remarks about her mother, eyes and father were read and not used.

Thomas H. Johnson and Theodora Ward (eds.), The Letters of Emily Dickinson, vol. II (Cambridge, Mass.: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 1958; 2nd printing 1965), archive.org lending-library OCR (lettersofemilydi0002unse_n7h2; catalogued there as 1914), read by line ranges -- SCHOLARLY EDITION perspective (modern editors working from the manuscripts, with manuscript, dating and publication notes); in-copyright, consulted for research only and quoted minimally. Read: no. 238 (summer 1861: two successive second stanzas of 'Safe in their Alabaster Chambers' sent to Susan Gilbert Dickinson, Susan's written reply that she was 'not suited' with the new stanza and thought the first complete in itself, and ED's third attempt, 'Is this frostier?', with the editors' manuscript note, HCL B 74a-c and 203d); the editors' notes and texts for nos. 260-261, 265, 268 (Higginson letters of 1862, incl. 'I smile when you suggest that I delay "to publish"'), no. 316 (early 1866: her complaint that 'The Snake' printed in the Springfield Republican of 14/17 Feb. 1866 was 'robbed of me -- defeated too of the third line by the punctuation ... I had told you I did not print'; editors' note on the Daily and Weekly Republican printings), the 1870 section introduction and nos. 338-342b (Higginson's visit), nos. 476a-c (Helen Hunt Jackson's Aug. 1876 letter enclosing the No Name Series circular and her call of 10 Oct. 1876; Higginson's reply of 22 Oct. 1876 that she need not do it if she felt a strong unwillingness), and the notes to no. 573 with Helen Hunt Jackson's letters to ED of 29 April and 25 Oct. 1878 and 8 Dec. 1878 and Thomas Niles's letter of 15 Jan. 1879 (nos. 573a-d: Jackson's repeated requests, offering to copy poems in her own hand so no one would know the author; 'Success' printed in A Masque of Poets 1878 'slightly changed in phraseology'; ED received the Jacksons in Oct. 1878, which the editors call unprecedented for her at that date). Jackson's and Niles's letters are contemporary NON-SELF documents (Jackson a friend and fellow author, Niles the publisher).

Martha Dickinson Bianchi, The Life and Letters of Emily Dickinson (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1924), archive.org OCR (lifelettersofemi00unse), read by line ranges (the chapters on the 1850s-60s and the later years, OCR lines c. 2380-2410, 3330-3350 and 3810-3830, plus keyword searches) -- FAMILY INSIDER perspective (niece, b. 1866, daughter of Susan and Austin Dickinson; partisan in the family-Todd editorial dispute and romanticising in tone; much of her account is family tradition rather than her own observation). Used ONLY as corroboration: her statement that Dickinson 'was always eager to respond to Susan's criticism', with her version of the 'Safe in their alabaster chambers' exchange (derived from the same Susan Dickinson papers as Johnson no. 238, so not independent of it), and her description of work done 'in secret and often at midnight'. Her suggestions about a love attachment behind the withdrawal were read and deliberately NOT used.

MacGregor Jenkins, Emily Dickinson: Friend and Neighbor (Boston: Little, Brown, 1930), archive.org OCR (emilydickinsonfr00jenk), read pp. 1-60 by line ranges -- CHILDHOOD NEIGHBOUR perspective (non-self; son of the Amherst pastor Rev. Jonathan Jenkins, he knew her as a child in the 1870s and recalls her half a century later; affectionate and anecdotal). Read: the gingerbread lowered in a basket from her window to the neighbourhood children; her pencilled notes and verses sent to the children; his remark that every scrap he handled showed 'haste to get the thing said while it was hot' while 'nothing with Miss Emily was haphazard'. Treated as low-weight colour; used only as minor corroboration that she circulated pencilled notes and verses privately rather than publishing; not used as support for any score on its own.

Emily Dickinson's OWN letters -- SELF perspective, counted as ONE perspective and never sole support for a row: to T. W. Higginson, 15 April, 25 April, 7 June and July 1862, Aug. 1862 ('Are these more orderly?'), 1862-63 wartime letters, early 1866 (no. 316, on 'The Snake' and 'I had told you I did not print'), 1869 ('I do not cross my Father's ground to any House or town'), c. 1872 and 1876 letters asking him to back her refusals (charity request; Helen Hunt Jackson's No Name request) -- as printed by Higginson (the record of Higginson's 1891 Atlantic Monthly essay) and by Johnson and Ward (the record of the Johnson and Ward edition of the letters, nos. 260-268, 316, 330); to Susan Gilbert Dickinson, summer 1861 (no. 238, the revised stanzas of 'Safe in their Alabaster Chambers'); and the girlhood letter to Abiah Root of 1848 (L20) as quoted by the Emily Dickinson Museum. Statements about her own illness, eyes, bereavements, the 'terror since September', and family members' feelings were read and not used.

Poetry Foundation, 'Emily Dickinson' biography page (poetryfoundation.org/poets/emily-dickinson; unsigned scholarly biography citing Sewall and the Johnson editions), fetched with curl 2026-10-02 and read in full -- SCHOLAR/EDITORIAL perspective, modern and independent of the 1890s editors. Used: Higginson's own letter to Atlantic editor James T. Fields written the day after receiving her first poems in April 1862 ('Two such specimens of verse as came yesterday & day before -- fortunately not to be forwarded for publication!'), as quoted there (a contemporaneous NON-SELF document; Higginson found the verse poorly structured and counselled her to wait before publishing); its account of the 'Alabaster Chambers' second stanza being reworked 'again, and yet again' in 1861; its note that she began organising poems into fascicles in 1858; and its view that restricting social visits was a practical choice that freed time for writing (treated as scholarly interpretation, not used as support). Its passages on the Susan Dickinson relationship, the 'Master' and the Todd-Austin affair were read and deliberately NOT used.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_dickinson_higginson_1891, src_dickinson_johnson_letters, src_dickinson_todd_prefaces, src_dickinson_edm_poet_at_work, src_dickinson_self_letters | 1862; 1866; 1876; 1878; c.1880-83; 1884 | correspondent + scholarly edition (incl. contemporary letters of H. H. Jackson and T. Niles) + editor + museum + self] She kept control over whether and how her poems circulated, against repeated outside pressure. In June 1862 she answered Higginson's advice to delay publishing that publishing was 'foreign to my thought'. Higginson records that when friends urged her to publish he 'was sometimes put forward as a defense', printing her letters declining a charity's request and, in Oct. 1876, Helen Hunt Jackson's request for the No Name Series. Jackson's own letters of 1878 (printed by Johnson and Ward) show her offering to copy poems in her own hand so that no one would know the author; her letter of 5 Sept. 1884 (quoted by Todd) still reproaches her that 'you will not give them light'. The Emily Dickinson Museum records that she avoided answering the publisher Thomas Niles, and that she instead shared about 500 poems privately with more than forty correspondents while keeping over 800 in hand-made booklets. In early 1866 she wrote to Higginson that the Springfield Republican's printing of 'The Snake' had been 'robbed of me'. Counter-evidence kept in view: she did let Jackson send 'Success' to A Masque of Poets (1878) and in c. 1880 selected poems for the charity; the museum notes no one knows for sure whether she wanted to publish. Dual-edged: almost none of her work reached print in her lifetime, and the posthumous editions were altered by others. Scored on control of her work, not on her seclusion.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_dickinson_higginson_1891, src_dickinson_poetryfoundation, src_dickinson_edm_biography, src_dickinson_self_letters | 1847-48; 1850s-1868; 1862-86 | correspondent + scholar (quoting Higginson's contemporaneous letter) + museum + self] In April 1862 Higginson, the established critic she had chosen to consult, privately told the Atlantic's editor Fields that the verse was not fit to be forwarded for publication (letter quoted by the Poetry Foundation biography) and offered criticism toward 'rules and traditions'; yet Higginson records that she would not change a line's word order to gain a rhyme ('she was intent upon her thought'), that she corrected a misspelling but left the 'greater irregularities' he pointed out, and that he 'soon abandoned all attempt to guide' her, though she went on calling herself his 'scholar' until 1886. Outside her writing, the Emily Dickinson Museum records, from the seminary's own journal, that at Mount Holyoke in 1847-48 she remained among the 29 students who had not professed faith by the end of the year, and that during the Amherst revivals, when family and friends made the public profession needed for church membership, she did not, and had stopped attending services by 1868. Her own letter of 1848 (L20) describes not yet having 'given up' while 'many are flocking'. Overlaps with autonomy_need; scored here on judgement held against advice and prevailing practice, not on publication.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_dickinson_higginson_1891, src_dickinson_todd_prefaces, src_dickinson_johnson_letters, src_dickinson_edm_poet_at_work, src_dickinson_poetryfoundation | 1862; 1866; 1878; 1890-94 | correspondent + editor + scholarly edition + museum + scholar] Scored from how far her documented practice departed from the conventions of her time, shown by what editors kept changing. Higginson (1891) describes her habitual dashes in place of punctuation, capitals on nouns and her 'defiance of form, never through carelessness', and says he regularised these when printing; his April 1862 letter to Fields (quoted by the Poetry Foundation) shows that the leading critic she consulted judged the verse unpublishable. The Springfield Republican altered the punctuation of 'The Snake' (1866), which she protested (Johnson and Ward note to no. 316), and Niles told her in Jan. 1879 that 'Success' had been 'slightly changed in phraseology' for A Masque of Poets. Todd's 1891 preface states that she 'intentionally avoided the smoother and more usual rhymes'; Todd (1894) restored 'dashes and capitals ... to their conventional use'; the museum records that the 1890 editors regularised punctuation, added titles and altered words for rhyme. Not scored from her later reputation or the number of poems.

experimentation.rationale: [src_dickinson_johnson_letters, src_dickinson_poetryfoundation, src_dickinson_todd_prefaces, src_dickinson_edm_poet_at_work, src_dickinson_bianchi_1924 | summer 1861; 1858-86 | scholarly edition (incl. Susan Dickinson's contemporaneous note) + scholar + editor + museum + family] In summer 1861 she sent Susan Gilbert Dickinson one version of 'Safe in their Alabaster Chambers', then an entirely different second stanza ('Perhaps this verse would please you better'), and after Susan's written reply that she was 'not suited' with it, a third ('Is this frostier?'); the manuscripts are at Harvard (Johnson and Ward no. 238; the Poetry Foundation describes the stanza reworked 'again, and yet again'; Bianchi gives a family version derived from the same papers). Todd, working from all the manuscripts in 1891, found many poems carrying lists of alternative words and phrases, and different versions in the copies sent to different friends; the museum records retained copies, unbound 'sets' and about 100 worksheets and fragments. Kept moderate: the evidence shows trying alternatives rather than a documented programme of formal experiment.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_dickinson_johnson_letters, src_dickinson_todd_prefaces, src_dickinson_self_letters, src_dickinson_jenkins_1930 | 1861; 1866; 1858-64 | scholarly edition + editor + self + neighbour] Some documented reworking and care over finished form: the three successive second stanzas of 'Safe in their Alabaster Chambers' in 1861 (Johnson and Ward no. 238), Todd's 1891 report that many fascicle poems 'had received thoughtful revision', and her 1866 objection that a single punctuation change by the Springfield Republican had 'defeated' a line of 'The Snake' (her own letter, with the editors' note confirming the printing). Counter-evidence kept in view: Todd says many poems 'bear evidence of having been thrown off at white heat', variant words were often left unresolved rather than settled, and Jenkins (1930) recalls notes written in haste 'while it was hot'. Moderate score and confidence; impact neutral.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_dickinson_edm_biography, src_dickinson_edm_poet_at_work, src_dickinson_todd_prefaces, src_dickinson_johnson_letters, src_dickinson_self_letters | c.1839-48; 1858-64; 1866 | museum + editor + scholarly edition + self] Three separate kinds of evidence. As a schoolgirl she assembled a herbarium of more than 400 pressed specimens, each labelled with its Latin name, now at Harvard's Houghton Library (Emily Dickinson Museum). In 1858-64 she fair-copied more than 800 poems onto folded sheets and bound them herself into forty booklets (museum); Todd, who handled them, describes the poems as 'carefully copied'. In early 1866 she wrote to Higginson that the Springfield Republican's printing of 'The Snake' had been 'defeated too of the third line by the punctuation' (self; Johnson and Ward's note confirms the Daily and Weekly printings of that February). Counter: Higginson notes she 'took pains to correct the spelling of a word' while ignoring larger irregularities, and her handwriting and pencil copies often troubled her editors.

discipline.rationale: [src_dickinson_edm_poet_at_work, src_dickinson_edm_biography, src_dickinson_todd_prefaces, src_dickinson_poetryfoundation, src_dickinson_bianchi_1924 | 1858-1865 | museum + editor + scholar + family] The documented working record shows sustained self-directed work without any outside deadline, editor or audience: from about 1858 she organised poems into fair-copied groups, and by 1864 had copied more than 800 into forty booklets she made herself, plus fifteen unbound 'sets' (museum; Poetry Foundation; Todd's 1891 description of the bundles). The museum, citing her niece, places her formal writing at a work table in her own bedroom, working late into the night; Bianchi describes the work as done 'in secret and often at midnight'. Kept moderate: no independent witness describes a daily routine, Bianchi's account is family tradition, and the museum notes she stopped formal assembly of booklets after the mid-1860s.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_dickinson_higginson_1891, src_dickinson_johnson_letters, src_dickinson_bianchi_1924, src_dickinson_self_letters | 1861; 1862-1886 | correspondent + scholarly edition (incl. Susan Dickinson's contemporaneous note) + family + self] She sought critical judgement of her craft from readers she respected. In April 1862, prompted by his Atlantic article, she wrote unsolicited to Higginson, a stranger, asking whether her verse was 'alive' and to be told 'what is true'; in July 1862 she asked him to 'tell me my fault, frankly as to yourself, for I had rather wince than die', and later that year asked 'Are these more orderly?'. Higginson records that she kept up the stance of his 'Scholar' in letters until her death in 1886. In 1861 she sent Susan Dickinson successive versions of a stanza in response to Susan's written criticism (Johnson and Ward no. 238; Bianchi, from family papers: 'always eager to respond to Susan's criticism'). Not scored higher because the requests come largely from her own letters, and Higginson's account shows she seldom adopted the specific advice.

curiosity.rationale: [src_dickinson_edm_biography, src_dickinson_higginson_1870_wife, src_dickinson_higginson_1891, src_dickinson_self_letters | c.1839-48; 1847-48; 1862; 1870 | museum + correspondent (contemporaneous notes) + self] The Emily Dickinson Museum documents wide reading beyond her household's shelves (the Brontes, the Brownings, George Eliot, Emerson, Hawthorne, Carlyle, De Quincey), a reading group that read Shakespeare aloud, daily reading of the Springfield Republican and every issue of the Atlantic Monthly, and a school-years herbarium of more than 400 specimens; at Mount Holyoke she wrote of being 'all engrossed in the history of Sulphuric Acid' (self, L22, quoted by the museum). Higginson's notes written on the night of 16 Aug. 1870 record her account of the first borrowed novel ('This then is a book! And there are more of them!'), and her letters ask him for books and articles she had not yet found (1862, 1870). Self-reported enthusiasm is used only as corroboration of the museum's documented reading.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_dickinson_edm_biography, src_dickinson_higginson_1870_wife, src_dickinson_higginson_1891, src_dickinson_todd_prefaces, src_dickinson_self_letters | 1842-1886; 1870; 1880s | museum + correspondent + editor + self] She gardened throughout her life, from age eleven ('My Plants grow beautifully', L3) to her last years, raising plants year-round in the conservatory added to the Homestead (Emily Dickinson Museum); she sent flowers with poems to friends to mark births, illness and condolences (museum), and Higginson records flowers and fragrant leaves sent with verses to his wife. Higginson's same-night letter of 16 Aug. 1870 describes her greeting him with two day-lilies ('These are my introduction') and records her stated test of poetry as a physical response. Higginson (1891) noted 'a rare and delicate sympathy with the life of nature' in her 1862 poems, and Todd (1894), reading all her letters, describes close attention to birds, insects, weather and seasons. Admiring witnesses throughout, hence moderate confidence.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_dickinson_higginson_1891, src_dickinson_johnson_letters, src_dickinson_edm_poet_at_work, src_dickinson_self_letters | 1876; c.1880-83 | correspondent + scholarly edition + museum + self] Low score = a pattern of declining requests indirectly rather than by direct refusal. Higginson writes that when she was urged to publish 'I was sometimes put forward as a defense', and prints two of her letters: one recounting that she 'hesitated' when a stranger pressed her for poems for a charity and turned to him; the other (Oct. 1876, dated by Johnson and Ward no. 476) asking him for 'a note saying you disapproved it, and thought me unfit' so that Helen Hunt Jackson, whom she would 'regret to estrange', would accept her refusal. The Emily Dickinson Museum records that when the publisher Thomas Niles raised a collection she 'avoided giving an answer'. Counter-evidence: she did state her unwillingness to Jackson in person ('I told her I was unwilling') and protested the 'Snake' printing in writing (1866). Moderate confidence; impact neutral.

provenance.notes: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-02) for Q4441 returned en label 'Emily Dickinson', description 'American poet (1830-1886)', ko label '에밀리 디킨슨', ko description '미국 시인', born 1830-12-10, died 1886-05-15 (each also with a year-precision duplicate), citizenship Q30 (United States), P18 'Emily Dickinson daguerreotype (Restored, cropped, blown up, sepia).jpg' (not used), enwiki 'Emily Dickinson', kowiki '에밀리 디킨슨' (used for displayNames ko-KR). Tags independent and late_recognition (her work was printed almost entirely after her death) and archetypes creative_creator + independent_creator are existing ids (en.ts); no new tags or occupations. EVIDENCE READ (8 substantive source records plus 2 orientation; all texts downloaded to scratch_r41/work/emily-dickinson and read locally by line ranges): Higginson, 'Emily Dickinson's Letters' (Atlantic Monthly Oct. 1891; read in full in its 1909 reprint, Carlyle's Laugh ch. XIX); Higginson's same-night letters to his wife and diary entry of 16-17 Aug. 1870 (as printed in Johnson and Ward); Johnson and Ward, The Letters of Emily Dickinson vol. II (1958, lending-library OCR; nos. 238, 260-268, 316, 338-342b, 476a-c, 573a-d and notes); Todd's preface to Poems, Second Series (1891) and 'Introductory' to Letters (1894); Emily Dickinson Museum 'Poet at Work' pages (five) and biography/special-topics pages (six); Poetry Foundation biography; Bianchi, Life and Letters (1924), selected passages; MacGregor Jenkins, Friend and Neighbor (1930), pp. 1-60. Dickinson's own letters are recorded as one SELF source (src_dickinson_self_letters) and never support a row alone. NOT READ / NOT USED: the Emily Dickinson Archive (edickinson.org returned an empty 202 response, not pursued); Johnson vol. I (no accessible text); Sewall and Habegger biographies (not freely available; only as cited by the museum); Bingham's Ancestors' Brocades (not read); Higginson's 1890 preface to the first series (not located in the downloaded copy, which is the Second Series). INDEPENDENT PERSPECTIVES: (1) Dickinson herself (letters) -- self, one perspective; (2) T. W. Higginson, her correspondent of 24 years and 1870 visitor -- contemporaneous private letters to his wife (1870) plus his retrospective 1891 essay (same witness, counted once; an admirer and posthumous co-editor, so interested); (3) Mabel Loomis Todd, editor who worked from all the manuscripts (interested party, did not know her face to face); (4) Thomas H. Johnson and Theodora Ward, modern scholarly editors, whose edition also prints contemporaneous NON-SELF letters by Susan Dickinson (1861), Helen Hunt Jackson (1876, 1878) and the publisher Thomas Niles (1879); (5) the Emily Dickinson Museum (modern museum scholarship citing Franklin, Johnson, Habegger, Sewall, Leyda); (6) the Poetry Foundation biography (modern scholarly biography; quotes Higginson's April 1862 letter to Fields); (7) Martha Dickinson Bianchi, niece (family insider, partisan; corroboration only); (8) MacGregor Jenkins, childhood neighbour (late memoir; corroboration only). NON-SELF behavioural sources: Higginson (both records), Todd, Johnson and Ward incl. the Susan Dickinson, Jackson and Niles letters, the Museum, the Poetry Foundation; Bianchi and Jenkins as minor corroboration. No adversarial contemporary source exists beyond Higginson's dismissive April 1862 letter to Fields and Susan Dickinson's critical 1861 note; most witnesses are admirers or editors with interests, so (per the Roster40 calibration lesson) all scores are below 85 and all confidences at or below 0.68. EPISODE USE (no episode supports more than two rows): Higginson correspondence of 1862 (rules/rhyme, abandoned guidance, Fields letter) -> independent_thinking, creative_originality; her requests for frank criticism and the 'Scholar' stance 1862-86 -> mastery_orientation; refusals and deflections of publication requests (1862 reply; 1876 Jackson; charity c.1880; Niles; 1884 Jackson letter) -> autonomy_need, conflict_tolerance; 'The Snake' printing and her 1866 complaint -> detail_orientation, autonomy_need; 1861 'Alabaster Chambers' revisions with Susan -> experimentation, mastery_orientation (the same exchange is also cited as one strand in perfectionism, so it is held to these as primary and perfectionism is scored low-moderate with explicit counter-evidence); manuscript variants and alternative words (Todd 1891, museum) -> experimentation, perfectionism; fascicle copying 1858-64 -> discipline, detail_orientation; editors' regularisation of punctuation, capitals and rhymes (Todd 1894, museum, Niles 1879) -> creative_originality; Mount Holyoke 1847-48 and non-profession of faith -> independent_thinking only; school herbarium -> detail_orientation, curiosity; reading (museum) and Higginson's 1870 notes on books -> curiosity; lifelong gardening, flowers sent with poems, the 1870 day-lilies -> aesthetic_sensitivity. ROWS CONSIDERED AND LEFT UNSCORED: achievement_drive and impact_motivation (whether she wanted publication or fame is genuinely disputed -- the museum states no one knows -- and her own statements point both ways); persistence (would rest on output volume over decades with little recognition -- an output count, not behaviour); deep_focus (rests on interpretation of her retired life, which the brief excludes); social_assertiveness (mixed: she wrote unsolicited to Higginson and talked 'continuously' in 1870, yet avoided meeting strangers -- and scoring it would lean on her seclusion); belief_updating (she solicited criticism but seldom adopted it; mixed); execution_speed (rapid drafting per Todd and Jenkins vs. long revision; contradictory); collaboration, leadership_drive, risk_tolerance, planning_orientation, competitiveness, persuasiveness, opportunity_sensing, decisiveness, adaptability, analytical_rigor, systems_abstraction, cross_domain_range -- no on-point evidence. EXCLUDED ON PURPOSE: all health material (the 1864-65 Boston eye treatment, the 'terror since September', her final illness) -- used only for dates of travel, never for personality; her seclusion is described only as documented behaviour and not scored or explained; no romance speculation (the 'Master' letters, Susan Dickinson, Judge Otis Lord, Samuel Bowles) -- the Susan exchange of 1861 is used only for its literary revision; Bianchi's suggestion of a love attachment, and the Todd-Austin Dickinson relationship; her father's character and family dynamics; her religious views beyond the documented fact that she did not make the public profession of faith; Todd's and Bianchi's characterisations of her temperament; Higginson's 1891 impression of 'an excess of tension, and of something abnormal' and his 1870 remark that she 'drained my nerve power' (psychological impressions, not used); no 'greatest poet' or first/only claims. KNOWN LIMITS: most sources are admirers, editors or family with interests in her reputation; Higginson's 1891 essay is retrospective (though the 1870 letters to his wife corroborate the visit); Todd never met her; the museum pages are short summaries citing secondary scholarship; the Johnson and Ward edition is in copyright and was consulted through a lending-library OCR and quoted minimally; the Poetry Foundation page is unsigned. Many dates of her letters are editors' estimates. PORTRAIT: the c. 1846-47 daguerreotype, the only authenticated photograph of Dickinson, original in Amherst College Archives & Special Collections (Millicent Todd Bingham gift, 1956; provenance per the Amherst College page 'The Dickinson Daguerreotype', https://www.amherst.edu/mm/284669, read 2026-10-02: from Lavinia Dickinson to Austin Baxter Keep in the 1890s, then Wallace Keep, then Bingham; conserved at George Eastman House in 1978). Commons file 'ED-dag-cropped-720dpi.tif' (uploaded 7 July 2016 by Mkelly5017, then replaced with the uncropped case scan the same day): Amherst's own 720 dpi colour scan of the open case, 4788 x 2797 px TIFF; wikitext read 2026-10-02: source 'Emily Dickinson Collection, Amherst College Archives & Special Collections', author {{unknown photographer}}, licence {{PD-old-70-1923}}, with the line 'This image is in the public domain. Please credit Amherst College Archives & Special Collections as the source of the original.' The same scan (ED-dag-case-720dpi.jpg) is displayed on Amherst's page, which states 'This image is in the public domain and Amherst College claims no authority over its use and reproduction' and 'we do not charge any use fees or claim any rights in this image', asking only that users cite Amherst College ASC as holder of the original. CAVEAT recorded for the lead: the same Amherst page also carries a site-template CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 badge said to apply to 'our reproduction of the original'; since Amherst disclaims all rights in the image in the preceding sentences, and the reproduction is a flat scan of a pre-1850 photograph by an unknown photographer (public domain in the US as an anonymous work over 120 years old), the basis is judged sound, but the lead may wish to note it. The original TIFF was downloaded and opened with PIL (4788 x 2797 RGB); the case lid, velvet and outer case border were cropped away, keeping the plate within its gold mat (crop box 2700,400-4325,2375 = 1625 x 1975 px), then downscaled to 1316 x 1600, JPEG q85; no restoration or retouching. Visually confirmed: seated young woman with centre-parted hair, ribbon at the collar, hand resting on a book on a patterned table cloth, holding flowers -- the known Dickinson daguerreotype, with its scratches. kind likeness. REJECTED: Wikidata P18 'Emily Dickinson daguerreotype (Restored, cropped, blown up, sepia).jpg' (heavily altered and enlarged derivative); 'Emily Dickinson daguerreotype.jpg', '(Unrestored)', '(Restored)' and '(cropped)' (617-619 px copy photographs from the Yale Todd-Bingham picture collection, low resolution, a copy of a copy); '(Restored and retouched).png' (retouched); 'Black-white photograph of Emily Dickinson2.png/.jpg' (a PNG re-encode of the same Amherst scan with only PD-US/PD-100 tags -- the Amherst-uploaded TIFF is the better-documented original); 'Emily Dickinson (perhaps) 1859.png' and 'Dickinson and Turner 1859' (the disputed 1859 daguerreotype, not authenticated). No eligibility, coverage or match output was used in scoring. PUBLICATION DECISION (lead review, frozen before any eligibility computation): evidence_approved -- an honest, evidence-backed profile with >=2 independent provenance perspectives and >=1 substantive non-self behavioural source. Portrait rights-verified. LEAD REVIEW (manual QA): internal source ids referenced inside source titles replaced by readable record names, since titles render on the public Sources list.
